claims.text: The alloy's combination of low density, mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance arises from spontaneous formation of a dual-phase microstructure.
Multicomponent alloy design promotes spontaneous formation of the dual-phase microstructure.
One phase is enriched in oxide-forming elements.
The oxide-former-enriched phase rapidly develops a stable protective passive film at high temperatures and in corrosive environments.
A second phase maintains high mechanical strength through lattice distortion and nanocrystalline grain-boundary strengthening.
The interface between the passivating and mechanically robust phases mediates the proposed dual functionality.
Configurational entropy stabilizes a fine dual-phase microstructure in the multielement alloy.
The passivating phase promotes formation of a continuous, adherent oxide film that resists high-temperature oxidation and corrosion.
Lattice distortions in the mechanically robust phase enhance dislocation pinning and thereby maintain or improve strength.
An optimized passivating-element concentration will produce lower oxidation-scale growth than the baseline alloy.
An optimized passivating-element concentration will produce lower corrosion rates than the baseline alloy.
An optimized passivating-element concentration will maintain or increase mechanical strength relative to the baseline alloy.
Too little oxide-forming element prevents formation of a continuous protective phase.
Too much oxide-forming element disrupts continuity of the mechanically strengthening phase and may increase brittleness or density.
Extreme processing conditions can override formation of the entropy-stabilized microstructure and nullify the proposed synergy.
